children: A Texas lawyer is facing civil and criminal charges for allegedly orchestrating a Ponzi scheme involving four fraudulent securities offerings. A former advisor who was barred from the industry and became a podcast host is also facing charges for soliciting investors for two of those offerings.

The lawyer, David Gilchrist, 70, allegedly convinced around 20 victims to invest in partnerships and promissory notes purportedly related to investments in property-tax liens. Instead, authorities say that he used the money for personal expenses and to make Ponzi-like payments to earlier investors.

The Justice Department says that from April 2023 through January 2026, Gilchrist raised about $1.45 million from investors and returned about $789,000. The Securities and Exchange Commission alleges that the fraud began earlier, in 2021, and raised more than $1.85 million.

Gilchrist was scheduled to make an initial court appearance on Wednesday. Court records don't indicate that he has retained a lawyer in the matter. A phone number for his law practice appears to be out of service.

The SEC alleges that Christopher Novinger, the podcaster, facilitated the purported scheme by soliciting investors, arranging for transfers of money to Gilchrist, and falsely telling two investors that he had personally invested in one of the offerings. The SEC alleges that Novinger's conduct violated the commission's 2016 order barring him from the brokerage industry.

Novinger has never been registered with a brokerage firm, though he was previously registered as an insurance agent with Texas authorities. The 2016 ban stemmed from the allegedly fraudulent sales of life insurance products. Novinger settled that matter without admitting or denying wrongdoing. Court records don't indicate that he has retained a lawyer in the current action. He is only facing civil charges.

The Justice Department alleges that Gilchrist went to significant lengths to disguise his alleged fraud, including misleading SEC investigators. The criminal complaint, filed in federal court in Texas' Northern District, alleges that during the SEC investigation, Gilchrist produced a series of forged deeds that included stamps and signatures from actual Texas notaries, "none of whom authorized Gilchrist to use their credentials," the Justice Department says.

Gilchrist also allegedly enlisted a woman to identify homeowners and deliver cash to them as part of the scheme. "[D]ays before testifying before the SEC, Gilchrist appeared unannounced at the woman's home, told her husband that the FBI was looking for him and advised them to 'take a vacation' for a couple of years, potentially in Mexico," the Justice Department says.

He allegedly kept his victims at bay with occasional payments, misleading information, and "implausible excuses such as a government shutdown, an arson investigation, and a hurricane-relief deployment," according to the Justice Department.
He is facing charges of wire fraud, aggravated identity theft, and witness tampering.
